title: No blame to Cunda
hookLine: the smith's meal, and the Buddha's care that he not be blamed
carry: for one who gives, merit grows

cards: A cook makes dinner for a guest she admires. That night the guest gets sick. Even if the food had nothing to do with it, the cook lies awake.
Was it the fish? Should I have known? And if the guest died, that question could follow her for years.
On day eighty-one you heard about Cunda, the smith's son at Pava, who served the Buddha his last meal.
The Udana tells the same story in its eighth chapter, and keeps a detail that's easy to pass over: what the Buddha did about Cunda's feelings, while he himself was dying.

teach.h: A DISH NO ONE CAN NAME FOR SURE.
teach.b: Cunda invites the Buddha and the monks for a meal, and among the dishes is one called sukaramaddava. Nobody today knows for certain what it was. Its name has the word for pig in it.
The commentaries take it as tender pork; other readers have taken it as a kind of mushroom, or a herbal preparation. The text doesn't say.
The Buddha tells Cunda to serve that dish to him alone, and to bury what's left, since no one else could digest it. After the meal, a severe illness comes on him, with sharp pains.
He bears it, mindful, and travels on toward Kusinara. And on the road, sick and near the end, he thinks of Cunda.
Someone, he tells Ananda, might make Cunda feel remorse: it's your loss, Cunda, that the Teacher passed away after eating your food. So go and dispel it.
Tell him this, from me: two offerings of food bring equal and great fruit, more than any others. The meal after which the Teacher awoke, and the meal after which he passes into final release.
Cunda's act was good; it brings long life, beauty, happiness and honor.
Look at the care in that. Dying, the Buddha spends some of his last strength protecting a man from guilt that wasn't his. The verse says it plainly: for one who gives, merit grows.

how: Buddhist teachers often tell of Cunda's meal as an example of the Buddha's compassion at the end of his life, and tradition identifies the meal before the awakening as Sujata's offering of milk-rice.

games.q: you're the Buddha. you're gravely ill after a meal at a supporter's house. you're traveling on toward the place where you'll die. what do you do about Cunda?
o: say nothing; it's not his concern.
send Ananda to tell him his gift was one of the two greatest.
warn the monks about his cooking.
games.why: he foresees Cunda's remorse and sends word that his offering brings great fruit, equal to the meal before the awakening.

practice: Think of someone who might be blaming themselves for something that isn't really their fault: a parent, a coworker, a friend after a bad day, maybe even you.
Notice the weight they're carrying, and find one thing you could say, simply and truly, that would lift some of it, the way the Buddha sent word to Cunda. Hold that sentence, ready.

wordCard.voice: Cunda. The smith's son whose meal the Buddha ate before he died; the Buddha sent Ananda to tell him his offering was among the two greatest. Today's word.
